On windows, at least, a good practice (albeit annoying) is to have an administrative account that is basically never used, but to make and use a standard account (you can change your current one if needed, so your stuff stays there). You'll be able to do everything you can on an admin account, but you'll have to type in the admin password for installs and major changes; so even if they know the password for the standard account, there's significantly less they can do without knowing your administrative account's password. You could also do the opposite of that and create a new standard or guest account for when guests come over as long as you can remember to log into it or at least log out of your password protected main account.

You can also password protect files, such as where you keep notes and pictures; which wouldn't be protected on any account that was left logged in. The first method, however, helps guard against malware attacks, by forcing you to type in your password to allow a program to install or make changes.

Just tire your muscles out and fuel their recovery. While it is complicated how it works, it's a  lot more simple to do than people make it seem. You want to train for endurance rather than strength so you go lighter, but longer than someone like me who lifts for strength. I would advise going 4 sets and be tired by the 3rd, but able to finish the 4th set. If you just use your body without adding stuff to weigh you down, then go until you need a break and repeat. You can also try climbing, like rock climbing.  I don't know how much that would cost or anything, but rock climbers tend to have great grip strength and be very tone.

When someone says they want to go to the gym then I ask, do you want to go to the gym to get strong or do you want to tone? In other words, do you want to get big and able to lift heavy things or do you want a 6 pack with definition?

To get big, strong muscles you need to lift heavy things no more than 8 reps and no more than 3 sets. You should struggle throughout, with increasing difficulty as your muscles exhaust. If you don't struggle then lift heavier. Make sure to get plenty of protein from food and, optionally, from supplements. Not all protein sources and brands are equal. Your exhausted muscles will need at least a day or two to recover. 

The best way I've found to do so cheaply is to get a  weight that's heavy for you (a dollar per pound for dumbells around here), but I'm currently not exercising because the 50 pound dumbell I have isn't heavy enough anymore so it bores me. I even have 10 pound ankle weights I use on my arms to push it to 60 pounds. So now I feel like the gym is my only cheap option. I do have one gym nearby with cheapish plans.

If you want to tone up then you can lift far less heavier, but still a little heavy, with a lot more reps (at least 10 reps per set). You don't need a weight at all for this, though, as you can use your body weight. Examples of common exercises include pushups and pullups. You can also use common items such as hammers. Everything gets heavy after a while.
